::: {.callout-note .se-question appearance="simple"}
## The question

[Linear Algebra Problem - columns of $A$ are linearly independent $\Rightarrow$ $A^TA$ non-singular](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/2283360/linear-algebra-problem-columns-of-a-are-linearly-independent-rightarrow), asked by [PhysicsMathsLove](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/413179/physicsmathslove) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2017-05-16; [CC BY-SA 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/)):

> I am trying to go in this direction only. Is this proof correct? ($A$ is an $m \times n$ matrix). 
>
> I am considering the contrapositive of the statement:
>
>
>
> Suppose $A^TA$ is singular. 
> Then $\det (A^TA) =0$. 
> $\det(A^TA) = \det(A^T) \det(A)$ and since $\det (A^T) = \det(A)$, we must have $det(A) = 0$. In other words, the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent.   $\blacksquare$
:::

Notice that
$$A^TA v\cdot v = Av \cdot Av = \Vert Av \Vert^2$$
So if $A^TA v= 0$, what does this tell you about $Av$?
